Caption: 

# AI could send interest rates higher

Chair Kevin Warsh says the FOMC will be militant on inflation. “We will deliver on the 2% inflation target,” he said in his press conference this afternoon. “There’s no walking back from our responsibilities.”

He also voted today to leave interest rates unchanged, despite inflation remaining far above 2%.

Why the dissonance? The best way to reconcile above-target inflation with an unchanged fed funds rate is to believe in AI. 

Warsh is a believer. “AI is going to make almost everything cost less,” he [told](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-feds-future-kevin-warsh-7-17-25/id1480890290?i=1000717777753) CNBC last year. 

Not immediately, though. Warsh also says he expects that the current boom in AI capex will “increase measured prices” over the next year.

But he believes we should focus on what’s on the other side of these increases: an AI productivity boom that will lower prices. 

In the long term, Warsh is confident that AI will be "structurally disinflationary" — like the internet once was, but more so.

“This is the most productivity-enhancing wave of our lifetimes,” he [says](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6LtRcC-JgBI), “past, present and future.”

Not everyone agrees that this will lower interest rates.

Higher productivity typically means the economy can grow faster without risking a surge in inflation (and therefore higher interest rates). But AGI promises something close to _infinite_ productivity — machines that do virtually everything for us.

What might that do to interest rates?

A paper by AI researcher Caleb Maresca suggests the prospect of “transformative AI” (TAI) could set off a mad scramble for assets that would send interest rates soaring.

“Under baseline scenarios,” Maresca calculates, “one-year interest rates rise to 10-16%.”

16%!

That’s a big number — and it’s not because AI will cause GDP growth to be similarly big. “Evolving beliefs about TAI could create significant upward pressure on interest rates well before any techn

Crypto got the Fed decision it wanted on Wednesday. It held the gains for about an hour.

The Federal Reserve left its benchmark at 3.50%-3.75% in a 9-3 vote and Bitcoin pushed above $64,400 on the print. Chair **Kevin Warsh** then opened his press conference with the line that took the move back: [“There is no soft inflation target.”](https://thedefiant.io/news/markets/bitcoin-slips-below-usd64k-after-warsh-says-no-soft-inflation-target) BTC traded just under $64,000 at press time, up about 1% over 24 hours, according to CoinGecko. Ether was off 1.9% at $1,882 and Solana down 2% at $72.58.

Three dissents on a hold is a wide split for Warsh's first meeting in the chair, and the presser told rates desks he will defend the 2% target through the discomfort. Crypto spent most of July pricing a friendlier Fed. Wednesday repriced the chair.

*THE BIG ONE*

*😴 'Sleepy July': K33 says bitcoin spot volume on track for weakest month since late 2023*

CZ ( https://www.theblock.co/post/410017/sleepy-july-k33-says-bitcoin-spot-volume-on-track-for-weakest-month-since-late-2023?utm_campaign=website&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=theblocknewsletters )

*K33 Research* reports that July is on track to be bitcoin’s weakest month for spot trading volume since *November 2023*.

* Average daily *bitcoin spot volume* across tracked exchanges reached about $2.2 billion for the month, with the seven-day average at $2.1 billion.
* Bitcoin declined roughly 3% over the past week while remaining range-bound between $60,000 and $66,000.
* Derivatives activity stayed muted as *CME* bitcoin open interest hovered near multi-year lows around 100,000 BTC and perpetual futures open interest stalled near 300,000 BTC.
* The subdued trading levels reflect a broader summer slowdown in market activity according to K33 Head of Research Vetle Lunde.
